summary: This All About Circuits project article by Tim Youngblood (July 7, 2018) explains how to control a DC motor's speed and direction using an L298 H-Bridge IC driven by an Arduino Mega2560. It describes the H-bridge concept, the L298 pin connections and direction truth table, and provides Arduino sketch code that runs the motor clockwise for 3 seconds, brakes, then runs counter-clockwise for 3 seconds. Website navigation, related-content links and reader comments are boilerplate and were ignored.
one_line: A tutorial on driving a DC motor clockwise and counter-clockwise with an L298 H-Bridge IC and an Arduino.
key_facts: The article 'How To Control a DC Motor with an Arduino' was written by Tim Youngblood and dated July 07, 2018.
A DC motor normally has two leads, and connecting them directly to a battery makes the motor rotate; switching the leads reverses rotation.
An H-bridge is an electronic circuit that can drive a motor in both directions and uses four transistors arranged so the schematic looks like an 'H'.
The L298 can control the speed and direction of DC motors and stepper motors and can control two motors simultaneously.
The L298 has a current rating of 2A for each motor, and heat sinks are needed at these currents.
The hardware list for the tutorial includes one L298 bridge IC, one DC motor, one Arduino Mega2560, one breadboard and ten jumper wires.
In the tutorial, IN1 is connected to Arduino pin 8, IN2 to pin 9, and Enable1 (EN1) to PWM pin 2.
The truth table shows IN1=1, IN2=0 gives FORWARD, IN1=0, IN2=1 gives BACKWARD, and IN1=0, IN2=0 or IN1=1, IN2=1 gives BRAKE.
The sketch uses digitalWrite() for pins 8 and 9 and analogWrite() on pin 2 with a value of 255 to set motor speed.
The motor runs clockwise for 3 seconds, brakes for 1 second, runs counter-clockwise for 3 seconds, then brakes for 1 second.
The setup instructions say to connect the IC's 5V and ground to the Arduino's 5V and ground, and to connect SENS A of the IC to ground.
The article notes that the L298 datasheet is available at http://www.tech.dmu.ac.uk/~mgongora/Resources/L298N.pdf.
A commenter asked how to adapt the design to control a treadmill motor, and another commenter warned that the article does not specify the IC's motor supply voltage (Vs).
